**Jargon File entry** (catb.org, HTML edition):

**yak shaving**  
[MIT AI Lab, after 2000: orig. probably from a Ren & Stimpy episode.] Any seemingly pointless activity which is actually necessary to solve a problem which solves a problem which, several levels of recursion later, solves the real problem you're working on.

Source: http://catb.org/jargon/html/Y/yak-shaving.html

### Relevant results (concise sourcing)

1. **Jargon File (canonical)** — Same definition as above; tagged MIT AI Lab, after 2000, probably from *Ren & Stimpy*. http://catb.org/jargon/html/Y/yak-shaving.html

2. **ZVON.org index** — Points to the Jargon File glossary entry for “yak shaving” (online hacker Jargon File). https://zvon.org/comp/m/yak_shaving.html

3. **Levellers.ai** — MIT AI Lab slang; coined in the 1990s by Carlin J. Vieri after a *Ren & Stimpy* “Yak Shaving Day” bit; early written note by Jeremy H. Brown (Feb 2000) on the all-ai list; Jargon File later recorded it. https://www.levellers.ai/what-is/yak-shaving

4. **TechTarget** — Endless small tasks before the next project step; credited to Carlin J. Vieri (MIT, 1990s), inspired by *Ren & Stimpy*. https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/yak-shaving

5. **ITBroker.com** — Chain of prerequisite tasks before the real goal; generally credited to Vieri at the MIT AI Lab in the 1990s, from *Ren & Stimpy*. https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/yak-shaving

6. **Visual Thesaurus (Mike Pope, 2014)** — Annoying succession of tasks before the actual goal; cites MIT/Vieri and the Jargon File’s *Ren & Stimpy* note. https://www.visualthesaurus.com/cm/wc/heavy-lifting-and-shaving-yaks-corporate-lingo/

7. **DEV Community** — Sub-tasks that look unrelated but are needed to finish the real task; origin given as an MIT lab. https://dev.to/cerchie/tech-jargon-defined-what-is-yak-shaving-3hj8

8. **PCMag** — Trivial or sidetracking work programmers do alongside coding. (Origin note differs: it cites a Sega game, not the Jargon File / *Ren & Stimpy* account.) https://www.pcmag.com/encyclopedia/term/yak-shaving

fetched.title: What Is Yak Shaving? | ITBroker.com
fetched.content:
[Skip to content](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/yak-shaving#main)

Yak shaving is informal engineering slang for the chain of seemingly unrelated tasks you have to finish before you can do the thing you actually set out to do. To install a new firewall, you need a maintenance window; to get the window, you need a change ticket; to raise the ticket, you need an account in the change system; and so on, until you find yourself, figuratively, shaving a yak. The term is usually told with a grin, but it names a real reason IT projects run late and over budget.

## At a glance

- Yak shaving describes a recursive chain of prerequisite tasks standing between you and the real goal.
- Each step can be legitimate on its own; the problem is how many there are and that nobody planned for them.
- Common causes include missing access, unclear ownership, undocumented systems, approvals and old dependencies.
- For buyers, it shows up as delays, change orders and disputes over what was in scope.
- Discovery, explicit assumptions in the [statement of work](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/statement-of-work-sow) and early escalation help keep it in check.

## What problem it solves

Yak shaving is a problem to recognize rather than a tool, and the term is useful because it gives teams a shared name for it. When an engineer says “I’m yak shaving,” they mean the visible goal hasn’t moved because they are clearing something underneath it. Naming that helps managers and customers see where the time is going and decide, deliberately, whether the chain is worth finishing, worth paying someone else to clear or a sign the plan needs to change.

For buyers, the useful question is why the yaks were there in the first place. Many come from conditions that existed before the project started: credentials nobody can find, systems without documentation, accumulated [technology debt](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/technology-debt), unclear owners and approval steps nobody mentioned during the sales process.

## How it works

A typical chain on an IT project might look like this. A provider is hired to move a branch office to a new SD-WAN service. Before the device can go in, they need the current router’s configuration. The router’s admin password is unknown, so someone has to recover it. Recovery needs console access, which needs a site visit, which needs building access and an escort. Meanwhile, the new circuit can’t be activated until the landlord approves a riser. None of these tasks is the project, but each one blocks it.

Common sources of yaks:

- **Access and accounts.** Admin credentials, portal logins, VPN access, badges and site escorts.
- **Unknown current state.** Undocumented configurations, unlabeled cabling and systems nobody owns.
- **Dependencies on old systems.** Software too old to upgrade directly, or an integration that has to be rebuilt first.
- **Approvals and process.** Change boards, security reviews, purchase orders and landlord or carrier approvals. Good [IT change management](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/it-change-management) is worth having, but each step adds lead time.
- **Tooling.** Automation and [DevOps](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/devops) work often starts with building the pipeline, inventory or test environment before the first useful change.

## When it matters for buyers

- **Scoping.** Fixed-price projects are vulnerable when the statement of work assumes a clean starting point. List known prerequisites, who owns each one and what happens if one takes longer than expected.
- **Discovery.** A paid discovery phase, assessment or [proof of concept](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/proof-of-concept-poc) can surface many yaks before you commit to a full timeline and price.
- **Customer responsibilities.** Many delays come from tasks only the customer can do, such as granting access, approving changes or chasing a landlord. Name them in the SOW with target dates.
- **Change orders.** Agree in advance how unplanned prerequisite work is raised, priced and approved, so it isn’t absorbed silently or billed by surprise.
- **Inherited environments.** After an acquisition or a staff change, expect more yaks. See our [managed network services](https://www.itbroker.com/solutions/managed-network-services) page for help scoping network projects with a provider.

## Questions to ask vendors

- What prerequisites does this project assume, and which of them are our responsibility?
- What discovery will you do before committing to a timeline, and is it priced separately?
- Which tasks have caused delays on similar projects for other customers?
- How will you tell us when prerequisite work is blocking progress, and how quickly?
- How are change orders for unplanned prerequisite work raised and approved?
- What happens to the schedule and price if access, approvals or information from our side arrive late?

## How it differs from technology debt

[Technology debt](https://www.itbroker.com/resources/glossary/technology-debt) is the accumulated cost and risk of old systems, shortcuts and postponed upgrades. Yak shaving is the experience of working through a chain of prerequisites to get something done. The two are closely linked: technology debt is a common source of yaks, because old, undocumented or unsupported systems have to be fixed or understood before new work can proceed. But yak shaving can happen in a well-run environment too, through approvals, access requests and tooling setup, and paying down technology debt is itself a project that can involve plenty of yak shaving.

## Problems this helps with

- A simple-sounding project keeps stalling on tasks nobody planned for
- Vendor says the delay is waiting on access, accounts or approvals from us
- Change orders for prerequisite work that wasn't in the statement of work
- Engineers busy for weeks with little visible progress on the actual goal

## Frequently Asked Questions

Where does the term yak shaving come from?

It is generally credited to Carlin Vieri at the MIT AI Lab in the 1990s, inspired by a "Yak Shaving Day" segment in The Ren and Stimpy Show, and it spread through programming blogs in the 2000s. Some dictionaries list the origin as uncertain.

Is yak shaving always a bad thing?

No. Often the prerequisite tasks are genuinely necessary, and finishing them unblocks the real work. The term becomes a warning when the chain keeps growing without anyone checking whether the original goal still justifies it, or when it turns into a way of avoiding harder work.

How do we reduce yak shaving on IT projects?

Do discovery before committing to a fixed timeline, list prerequisites and customer responsibilities in the statement of work, give someone the job of clearing access and approvals early, and set a point at which unexpected prerequisite work is escalated instead of quietly absorbed.

Who pays for unplanned prerequisite work?

It depends on the contract. If the statement of work lists assumptions and customer responsibilities, work outside them usually becomes a change order. If the scope is vague, expect a dispute. Agree the change process before work starts.

![Andy Patrizio](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/patrizio_andy.jpg)

By

- [Andy Patrizio](https://www.techtarget.com/contributor/Andy-Patrizio)

Published: Jan 27, 2023

## What is yak shaving?

Yak shaving is programming lingo for the seemingly endless series of small tasks that have to be completed before the next step in a project can move forward. The term is a great example of internet slang making its way into the collective consciousness and being used to describe impediments to coding.

The term was coined by Carlin J. Vieri, a Ph.D. student at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the 1990s, and was inspired by an episode of the Nickelodeon channel's cartoon _The Ren & Stimpy Show_. In the episode, Ren informs the viewers of an upcoming holiday called Yak Shaving Day, where one must leave shaving cream and a razor on the bathroom sink so that, at night, the Shaven Yak can come and leave presents.

Of course, Vieri was being sarcastic, but the term _yak shaving_ caught on. It refers to engaging in a meaningless task that has no obvious relationship to what's supposed to be worked on but may be necessary to troubleshoot a larger problem. The process of making a simple task unnecessarily complicated may also qualify as yak shaving.

A yak is a domesticated, horned, cowlike mammal native to Tibet that looks similar to a Texas longhorn cow -- albeit with shorter horns -- but with a thick, shaggy coat to help cope with the cold climate of Tibet.

## Examples of yak shaving

Examples of yak shaving fall into two categories: procrastination and necessary annoyance. In the case of the former, it's easy to slip into while [working from home](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/feature/15-advantages-and-disadvantages-of-remote-work), where temptations and distractions abound.

For example, procrastination is when there's a report due today, but it seems dull and a waste of time because no one will ever read it. So, it falls to the end of the priority list behind other household chores -- anything to avoid writing the report.

Necessary annoyance occurs when the original goal is to complete task A, but an unforeseen cascade of circumstances intervenes to distract from completing it. Those involved with software development may be especially sensitive to necessary annoyances. For example, a field entry name must be changed in [source code](https://www.techtarget.com/searchapparchitecture/definition/source-code) because it was changed in the database. But, as the software engineer looks into the code, other errors become apparent and need to be corrected. The required changes affect other apps, and then those, in turn, affect yet more applications. That can lead a developer down a rabbit hole of [dependency hell](https://www.techtarget.com/searchitoperations/definition/dependency-hell) that needs to be fixed before making the initial modifications.

## How to avoid yak shaving

Avoiding both types of yak shaving requires self-discipline and self-awareness. In the case of procrastination, it comes down to recognizing it, stopping the time-wasting exercises and getting on with the unpalatable task at hand.

![Steps to avoid yak shaving](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/yak_shaving-f.png)Follow these steps to avoid falling down a rabbit hole.


In the case of distraction, stopping isn't an option because these are necessary steps. Even if a half-dozen other updates occur before making a planned change, they must be done.

It is possible to reduce the distracting effects of yak shaving by reframing the situation. Here are some steps to consider:

1. **Realize you have been sidetracked.** The moment you realize you are moving toward yak shaving, stop.
2. **Understand the task at hand.** You can't get back on track until you realize what the track is. Refocus to become aware of possible distractions.
3. **Have a plan of action.** Once you've recognized you are off course, formulate a [project plan](https://www.techtarget.com/searchcio/definition/project-planning) to get back on course.
4. **Set modest goals.** A series of small tasks is easier to accomplish than one giant task.
5. **Set periodic checkpoints.** Stop periodically to ensure you are still on the planned path.
6. **Have a better working environment.** This is ideal advice for avoiding procrastination: Reduce as many distractions and temptations as possible.

One method for setting periodic checkpoints is the [Pomodoro Technique](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/pomodoro-technique), which breaks work into 25-minute chunks punctuated by five-minute breaks.
